readings.title: First reading
readings.text: Through the Law I am dead to the Law, so that now I can live with God. I have been crucified with Christ, and I live now not with my own life but with the life of Christ who lives in me. The life I now live in this body I live in faith: faith in the Son of God who loved me and who sacrificed himself for my sake.

exegesis.summary: St. Paul testifies to the radical transformation worked by grace: through the Law's own witness he has died to the Law's power to condemn, and now lives a new life hidden in Christ. His life is no longer autonomous; Christ himself lives within him, and this indwelling is received and sustained by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him. Paul's 'crucified with Christ' is the paradigm of every baptized life.

patristicQuotes.quote: Though his flesh die, his soul shall live till the flesh rise again, never to die more. For faith is the life of the soul.
When I believed that Thou wert the Son of God, I believed that Thou wert the resurrection, that Thou wert life; and that he that believeth in Thee, though he were dead, shall live.

cccReferences.title: Crucified with Christ, led by the Spirit
Christ is the end of the Law
Faith by which man commits his entire self to God
New life carried in earthen vessels

exegesis.thematicConnection: Paul's confession that 'Christ lives in me' is the doctrinal expression of the Gospel's image of the vine and branches: the Christian's true life is not his own but Christ's, received by faith and abiding.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
I will bless the Lord at all times.
or
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
I will bless the Lord at all times,
his praise always on my lips;
in the Lord my soul shall make its boast.
The humble shall hear and be glad.
I will bless the Lord at all times.
or
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
Glorify the Lord with me.
Together let us praise his name.
I sought the Lord and he answered me;
from all my terrors he set me free.
I will bless the Lord at all times.
or
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
Look towards him and be radiant;
let your faces not be abashed.
This poor man called, the Lord heard him
and rescued him from all his distress.
I will bless the Lord at all times.
or
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
The angel of the Lord is encamped
around those who revere him, to rescue them.
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
He is happy who seeks refuge in him.
I will bless the Lord at all times.
or
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
Revere the Lord, you his saints.
They lack nothing, those who revere him.
Strong lions suffer want and go hungry
but those who seek the Lord lack no blessing.
I will bless the Lord at all times.
or
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
readings.refrain: I will bless the Lord at all times.

exegesis.summary: Psalm 34 is the song of the redeemed poor man whose whole existence has become blessing and praise. Because the Lord has heard him and delivered him, his lips overflow with thanksgiving, and he invites others to 'taste and see' the goodness of God. It is the natural voice of a soul that no longer lives for itself but for the Lord.

patristicQuotes.quote: He never refuses His blessings to them that pray, but rather stirs men up by His mercy not to faint in praying. Consider what a blessed privilege is granted thee, to talk with God in thy prayers.

cccReferences.title: Praise recognizes that God is God
Our heart is restless until it rests in you

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm gives voice to the soul in whom Christ lives (first reading) and who abides in the vine (Gospel): a life grafted into Christ inevitably becomes ceaseless blessing and boasting in the Lord.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text:
Jesus said to his disciples:
‘I am the true vine,
and my Father is the vinedresser.
Every branch in me that bears no fruit
he cuts away,
and every branch that does bear fruit
he prunes to make it bear even more.
You are pruned already,
by means of the word that I have spoken to you.
Make your home in me, as I make mine in you.
As a branch cannot bear fruit all by itself,
but must remain part of the vine,
neither can you unless you remain in me.
I am the vine,
you are the branches.
Whoever remains in me, with me in him,
bears fruit in plenty;
for cut off from me you can do nothing.
Anyone who does not remain in me
is like a branch that has been thrown away – he withers;
these branches are collected and thrown on the fire,
and they are burnt.
If you remain in me
and my words remain in you,
you may ask what you will
and you shall get it.
It is to the glory of my Father that you should bear much fruit,
and then you will be my disciples.’

exegesis.summary: On the eve of his Passion, Jesus reveals the intimate mystery of communion with himself: he is the true vine, his Father the vinedresser, and we the branches. Everything depends on remaining in him, for apart from him we can do nothing; united to him, we bear abundant fruit that glorifies the Father. Even the pruning — the sufferings and purifications of Christian life — is the Father's loving work to increase fruitfulness.

patristicQuotes.quote: He who thinks that he bears fruit of himself, is not in the vine; he who is not in the vine, is not in Christ; he who is not in Christ, is not a Christian.

He does not say, ye can do little. Unless the branch abides in the vine, and lives from the root, it can bear no fruit whatever. Christ, though He would not be the vine, except He were man, yet could not give this grace to the branches, except He were God.
By fruit is meant life, i.e. that no one can be in Him without good works.

cccReferences.title: The fruit is holiness of life made fruitful by union with Christ

exegesis.thematicConnection: The Gospel supplies the underlying reality that Paul confesses: the branch does not live by itself. 'Christ lives in me' (Galatians) is the same mystery as 'abide in me' (John), and its fruit is the ceaseless praise of Psalm 34.

synthesis.title: Abiding: The One Life That Bears Fruit
synthesis.body: Today the Church places before us a single truth from three angles. In the Gospel, Jesus discloses the innermost secret of Christian existence: 'I am the vine, you are the branches.' All fruitfulness — every good work, every holiness, every prayer that reaches the Father — flows from remaining grafted into him. 'Cut off from me you can do nothing,' he says plainly, and St. Augustine insists that this leaves no room for the illusion of self-sufficient goodness: 'He who thinks that he bears fruit of himself, is not in the vine.' St. Paul, in Galatians, gives us the personal confession of a branch that knows itself alive only in the vine: 'I live now not with my own life but with the life of Christ who lives in me.' The Law could not produce this; only being crucified with Christ and receiving his indwelling life by faith could. And Psalm 34 gives us the song such a life inevitably sings: 'I will bless the Lord at all times… Taste and see that the Lord is good.' The branch that abides is pruned, yes — sometimes painfully — but it blossoms into praise, into good works, into the glory of the Father. Today the Eucharist we receive is precisely this abiding made flesh: he in us and we in him, that we may bear much fruit.
